title: Does Coffee Dehydrate You? Calculator + Hydration Table | Hacé Cuentas
h1: Does Coffee Dehydrate You? The Real Numbers on Caffeine and Hydration
description: Coffee does NOT dehydrate you — it hydrates at ~90% of its volume. Calculate your net daily hydration from coffee and your total caffeine intake. See exactly how many mL you get and whether you're within the 400 mg/day safe limit.
answerSnippet: Coffee does NOT dehydrate you. It provides approximately 90% of its volume as net hydration. A 240 mL cup gives you ~216 mL of fluid. The safe caffeine limit is 400 mg/day (~4 standard cups of filter coffee). The dehydration myth dates to a flawed 1928 study using extreme doses in non-habitual drinkers.
intro: The idea that coffee dehydrates you is one of the most persistent health myths. Research shows the opposite: coffee is mostly water, and its net effect on your fluid balance is positive. The caffeine in a standard cup (~95 mg) does have a mild diuretic effect, but your body retains roughly 90% of the fluid you drink. A frequently cited 2014 trial in the *British Journal of Nutrition* (Killer et al.) found moderate coffee intake produced the same total body water as an equal volume of plain water in habitual drinkers.
keyTakeaway: Coffee contributes ~90% of its volume as net hydration. The dehydration myth stems from a 1928 study using extreme caffeine doses in people who had abstained for days — not representative of normal daily coffee drinking. At under 400 mg caffeine per day, coffee hydrates.

explanation:
## Does Coffee Dehydrate You? The Science

The dehydration myth dates to a 1928 study that administered large caffeine doses to people who had abstained from caffeine for several days. Under those extreme conditions, a transient diuretic effect was observed. In habitual coffee drinkers at normal doses, the effect is negligible — the body adapts to regular caffeine intake within days.

The definitive modern evidence: Killer et al. (2014) ran a controlled crossover trial in free-living adults and found **no significant difference in total body water** between days when participants drank 4 cups of coffee vs. the same volume of water.

## How the Calculator Works

### Net Hydration

Coffee retains approximately 90% of its volume as net hydration:

```
Net hydration (mL) = cups × mL_per_cup × 0.90
```

### Caffeine Estimate

A standard 8 oz (240 mL) brewed filter coffee contains roughly 70–140 mg caffeine, averaging ~95 mg:

```
Caffeine (mg) = cups × 95
```

*Note: espresso ~63 mg per 30 mL shot; instant coffee ~60 mg per 240 mL.*

### Safety Threshold

Both the FDA and EFSA identify **400 mg/day** as the caffeine amount not associated with adverse effects in healthy adults.

## Hydration Table: Cups of Coffee (240 mL each)

| Cups/day | Total volume | Net hydration | Caffeine est. | Within limit? |
|:--------:|:------------:|:-------------:|:-------------:|:-------------:|
| 1 | 240 mL | 216 mL | ~95 mg | ✅ Yes |
| 2 | 480 mL | 432 mL | ~190 mg | ✅ Yes |
| 3 | 720 mL | 648 mL | ~285 mg | ✅ Yes |
| 4 | 960 mL | 864 mL | ~380 mg | ✅ Yes |
| 5 | 1,200 mL | 1,080 mL | ~475 mg | ⚠️ Over 400 mg |
| 6 | 1,440 mL | 1,296 mL | ~570 mg | ❌ High |

## Net Hydration by Beverage Type

| Beverage | Net fluid retention | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Plain water | 100% | Reference |
| Coffee or black tea | ~90% | Mild, compensable diuretic effect |
| Green tea | ~95% | Lower caffeine than black tea |
| Herbal infusions | ~100% | Chamomile, peppermint, etc. |
| Soups and broths | ~95% | Also provide electrolytes |
| Regular soda | ~95% | Hydrates but adds sugar |
| Alcohol | Negative | Blocks ADH hormone — genuinely dehydrating |

## Disclaimer

This calculator provides a general estimate. Individual caffeine sensitivity varies. Pregnant individuals, people with certain heart conditions, and those on specific medications should consult a doctor about their caffeine intake.

faq.a: No. The frequently cited Killer et al. (2014) trial in the *British Journal of Nutrition* found that moderate coffee intake (4 cups/day) produces the same total body water as an equal volume of plain water in habitual drinkers. Caffeine has a mild, short-lived diuretic effect, but the fluid in the coffee more than compensates. Net result: coffee hydrates at approximately 90% of its volume.

faq.q: How much of the water in coffee does my body actually absorb?
faq.a: Approximately 90%. Because caffeine slightly increases urine output, the retention rate is a few percent lower than plain water, but the difference is negligible at typical intake levels. A 240 mL cup contributes roughly 216 mL to your fluid balance.

faq.q: What is a safe daily caffeine limit?
faq.a: Both the FDA and EFSA set the threshold at 400 mg per day for healthy adults — roughly 4 standard cups (240 mL) of filter coffee. Pregnant individuals are advised to stay under 200 mg/day. Above 400 mg, side effects such as anxiety, insomnia, and elevated heart rate become more common.

faq.q: How much caffeine is in espresso vs. filter coffee?
faq.a: A single espresso shot (~30 mL) contains around 63 mg of caffeine. A standard 240 mL drip coffee contains 70–140 mg, averaging ~95 mg. Espresso has more caffeine per mL but less per serving. This calculator uses 95 mg/cup as a representative average for filter coffee.

No. Tea has the same net hydrating effect as coffee. Black tea contains roughly 47 mg of caffeine per 240 mL cup — about half that of filter coffee — so the mild diuretic effect is even smaller. Green tea has even less caffeine. All teas are net-positive for hydration.

faq.q: Should coffee count toward my daily fluid intake goal?
faq.a: Yes. The U.S. National Academies and the NHS both acknowledge that all beverages — including coffee and tea — contribute to daily fluid intake. The common advice to drink 8 glasses of *water* is a simplification; total fluid from all sources, including food, is what matters.

faq.q: Can I replace all my water with coffee?
faq.a: Coffee hydrates, but using it as your sole fluid source is not practical or safe. To reach the ~2.5 L daily fluid target for an average adult using only 240 mL cups of coffee, you would need over 11 cups — delivering more than 1,000 mg of caffeine, more than double the safe limit. Drink water alongside your coffee.

faq.q: Does adding milk or sugar change the hydration calculation?
faq.a: Adding milk slightly increases total fluid volume, so your net hydration would be marginally higher than shown (the calculator only counts the coffee). Sugar has a negligible effect on hydration. The caffeine estimate remains the same regardless of additives.

faq.q: Does tolerance to caffeine change how it affects hydration?
faq.a: Yes. Habitual coffee drinkers develop tolerance to caffeine's diuretic effect within a few days of consistent intake. For regular drinkers, the diuretic effect is even smaller than the 10% assumed here, meaning net hydration may be slightly better than this calculator estimates.
